THERAPEUTIC DRUG MONITORING__Psychiatric:
Lithium is a mood stabiliser used for maintenance treatment of bipolar affective disorder (and as an antidepressant augmentation agent). It has a narrow therapeutic index — the gap between an effective level and a toxic level is small — so treatment is guided by regular serum lithium monitoring plus surveillance of the organs it damages (kidney, thyroid, parathyroid). The “test” is a timed serum level interpreted against a tight target range.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Lithium is monitored because it is renally cleared, has a narrow therapeutic window, and small shifts in fluid balance or renal function markedly change serum concentration. Too low and it is ineffective for relapse prevention; too high and it becomes neurotoxic and nephrotoxic.

Maintenance treatment of bipolar affective disorder (relapse prevention) — the classic indication.
Augmentation of antidepressants in treatment-resistant depression; also used in recurrent unipolar depression.
Anti-suicidal effect independent of mood stabilisation.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — SAMPLING

Timing is everything: the sample must be standardised to the trough phase of the dosing interval.

Serum sample taken exactly 12 h post-dose→Standardised trough level — the value the therapeutic range refers to
First check at steady state (~5–7 days after starting)→Recheck 1 week after every dose change until stable
Once stable→Serum lithium every 3 months (more often if elderly, renal impairment, or interacting drugs)
3BASELINE & ONGOING MONITORING

Because lithium damages the kidney, thyroid and parathyroid over time, organ bloods are done before starting and at intervals thereafter.

🧪U&Es / eGFR
Baseline then every 6 months — renal clearance drives levels; watch for CKD and DI
🦋TFTs
Baseline then every 6 months — lithium causes hypothyroidism
🦴Calcium
Baseline then every 6 months — can cause hyperparathyroidism / hypercalcaemia
⚖️Weight / BMI
Baseline and during treatment — weight gain is common
4INTERPRETATION, PITFALLS & SAFETY

The value is read against a tight target; rising levels map onto escalating toxicity.

0.4–1.0 mmol/L→Therapeutic range (0.6–0.8 mmol/L typical maintenance target)
>1.2 mmol/L→Above range — toxicity risk; review dose and precipitants
>1.5 mmol/L→Moderate toxicity — coarse tremor, GI upset (vomiting/diarrhoea), ataxia
>2.0 mmol/L→Severe toxicity — seizures, renal failure, coma; may need haemodialysis
Long-term use→Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism

Watch for precipitants that reduce clearance or cause dehydration — these push a therapeutic patient into toxicity:

Dehydration — D&V, hot weather, reduced intake.
NSAIDs — reduce renal lithium excretion.
ACE inhibitors / ARBs and thiazide diuretics — raise lithium levels.
Acute kidney injury from any cause.
🚩 Lithium toxicity is life-threatening. Suspect it with coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion, vomiting/diarrhoea, and seizures. Withhold lithium, check an urgent serum level and U&Es, and rehydrate with IV fluids. Consider haemodialysis if the level is >2.5 mmol/L or there are severe features. Avoid NSAIDs, thiazides and dehydration in anyone on lithium.
🎓 Sample serum lithium 12 h post-dose; therapeutic range 0.4–1.0 mmol/L (aim 0.6–0.8). Monitor U&Es and TFTs 6-monthly. NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and thiazides plus dehydration are the classic precipitants of toxicity.

Clozapine is the only antipsychotic licensed for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, but it can cause life-threatening agranulocytosis and myocarditis. For this reason every patient must be registered with a clozapine monitoring service, and full blood count (FBC) surveillance with a traffic-light neutrophil system is mandatory and non-negotiable throughout treatment.

1Indication & principle

Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia — inadequate response to an adequate trial of at least two antipsychotics (one being a second-generation agent). It has unique efficacy but a narrow safety margin.

Agranulocytosis (severe neutropenia) occurs in ~1–3% and can be fatal from overwhelming sepsis.
Risk of neutropenia is highest in the first 18 weeks, justifying the front-loaded monitoring schedule.
Myocarditis clusters in the first 6–8 weeks; cardiometabolic harm accrues over the long term.
2FBC monitoring scheme

Patient, prescriber and pharmacy are registered with a monitoring service; clozapine is dispensed only against an in-range FBC ("no blood, no drug").

Weekly FBC for the first 18 weeks.
Fortnightly from week 18 to 1 year.
Monthly (4-weekly) thereafter, continuing for the duration of treatment and for 4 weeks after stopping.

Results are graded by a traffic-light system based on the neutrophil count (WCC is also monitored):

Neutrophils >2.0 ×10&sup9;/L→GREEN — continue clozapine, routine monitoring
Neutrophils 1.5–2.0 ×10&sup9;/L→AMBER — continue but increase monitoring (repeat FBC twice weekly)
Neutrophils <1.5 ×10&sup9;/L→RED — STOP clozapine immediately, daily FBC, haematology input
3Beyond the FBC — other monitoring
🫀Myocarditis
First 6–8 weeks; check troponin, CRP & ECG if symptomatic
⚖️Metabolic
Weight, fasting glucose/HbA1c & lipids — weight gain and diabetes are common
🚽Constipation
Anticholinergic bowel hypomotility — can progress to ileus
🌡️Fever
Benign transient pyrexia is common early, but must not mask sepsis or myocarditis
Fever / sore throat / flu-like illness in first weeks→Urgent FBC — exclude neutropenic sepsis AND myocarditis
Tachycardia, chest pain, dyspnoea, ↑ troponin/CRP/eosinophils (weeks 1–8)→Clozapine myocarditis — stop drug, cardiology referral
4Pitfalls & safety
Benign ethnic neutropenia can trigger false alarms — a lower monitoring threshold may be agreed for eligible patients.
Smoking induces clozapine metabolism (CYP1A2); stopping smoking abruptly (e.g. hospital admission) can cause toxic levels.
If clozapine is missed for ≥48 hours it must be re-titrated slowly from a low dose — never restarted at the previous dose.
🚩 A RED result (neutrophils <1.5 ×10&sup9;/L) mandates immediate cessation and haematology input — clozapine agranulocytosis can be fatal. Clozapine myocarditis in the first 6–8 weeks presents with tachycardia, fever, chest pain and dyspnoea — check troponin, CRP and ECG. Severe constipation can progress to life-threatening ileus and must never be ignored.
🎓 High-yield: FBC monitoring is mandatory and dispensing is blocked without it. Neutrophils <1.5 = STOP. Suspect myocarditis in the first 2 months. After a break of ≥48 h, always re-titrate — never abruptly restart at the old dose.

Antipsychotic metabolic monitoring is a structured programme of physical-health surveillance for every patient started on an antipsychotic. It detects and pre-empts the drug-induced cardiometabolic and endocrine harms — weight gain, dysglycaemia, dyslipidaemia, QTc prolongation and hyperprolactinaemia — that make cardiovascular disease the leading cause of premature death in people with severe mental illness.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

All patients on antipsychotics require monitoring, but the burden is greatest with second-generation agents. Blockade of histamine H₁ and 5-HT₂₄ receptors drives appetite and weight gain; peripheral effects impair insulin sensitivity and worsen the lipid profile; dopamine D₂ blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway disinhibits prolactin release; and cardiac K⁺ (hERG) channel blockade lengthens the QT interval.

⚖️Olanzapine
Worst metabolic profile: marked weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidaemia
🩸Clozapine
Severe metabolic risk plus myocarditis; also needs FBC monitoring
🍽️Quetiapine
Moderate weight/metabolic effect; low prolactin burden
🥛Risperidone
Marked hyperprolactinaemia; moderate metabolic effect
🥛Amisulpride
Strong prolactin rise; also QTc prolonging
🍃Aripiprazole
Prolactin-sparing (partial agonist); low metabolic burden
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — THE MONITORING SCHEDULE

A baseline physical-health panel is taken before or at initiation, repeated at 12 weeks (when most weight gain and dysglycaemia emerge), then at least annually thereafter. Weight is checked more frequently in the early phase (e.g. weekly for the first 6 weeks then at 12 weeks). Bloods for glucose and lipids are ideally fasting.

Anthropometry: weight, BMI and waist circumference
Glycaemia: fasting plasma glucose or HbA1c
Lipids: total cholesterol, HDL, LDL, triglycerides
Cardiac: ECG for QTc (baseline, on dose change, and for QT-prolonging drugs)
Endocrine: serum prolactin (baseline and if symptomatic)
Vascular: blood pressure and pulse

Timing summary: baseline → 12 weeks → annually for weight, glucose, lipids and ECG.

3INTERPRETATION — VALUES & ACTIONS
Weight gain ≥5% / rising BMI + waist >102 cm (M) or >88 cm (F)→Metabolic syndrome & raised cardiovascular risk — lifestyle input, consider switch
Fasting glucose ≥7 mmol/L or HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol (rising trend)→Antipsychotic-induced diabetes (esp. olanzapine, clozapine) — treat, review agent
QTc >500 ms or increase >60 ms from baseline→Torsades risk — review/change drug (haloperidol, high-dose), correct electrolytes
Raised prolactin + galactorrhoea / amenorrhoea / sexual dysfunction→Hyperprolactinaemia (risperidone, amisulpride, typicals) — dose review or switch
On aripiprazole or quetiapine→Lower metabolic / prolactin burden — reasonable switch target if harm emerges
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Non-fasting glucose/lipid samples can mask true dysglycaemia and dyslipidaemia — repeat fasting where feasible.
QTc is rate-corrected; bradycardia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and hypocalcaemia all worsen risk and must be corrected.
Prolactin has a diurnal rhythm and rises with stress and venepuncture — a mildly raised isolated result should be repeated.
Monitoring is frequently omitted in practice; physical-health checks are as much a patient-safety priority as psychiatric review.
🚩 A QTc >500 ms or a rise >60 ms from baseline markedly increases the risk of torsades de pointes and sudden cardiac death — review and change the antipsychotic and correct electrolytes urgently. Actively screen for and treat emergent diabetes and dyslipidaemia: cardiometabolic disease, not suicide, is the leading cause of premature death in these patients.
🎓 Olanzapine and clozapine are the worst for metabolic harm — check weight, glucose, lipids and ECG at baseline, 12 weeks and annually. Risperidone and amisulpride raise prolactin; aripiprazole is prolactin-sparing and metabolically gentle.

Antidepressant review is a structured clinical review — not a serum-level test — used to judge whether an antidepressant is working, to catch adverse effects and safety concerns early, and to guide dose titration, switching or continuation. It underpins safe SSRI/SNRI prescribing in depression and anxiety.

1Indication & principle

Antidepressants take time to act: neurochemical changes (increased synaptic serotonin/noradrenaline) begin quickly, but clinical mood improvement is typically delayed. A therapeutic dose must be maintained long enough before response can be judged, so review balances efficacy against tolerability and safety.

Confirms benefit (improved mood, sleep, function) versus adverse effects.
Screens for emergent suicidality, especially early in treatment.
Detects drug-specific harms: hyponatraemia, GI bleeding, QTc prolongation.
2Review schedule & how it is done

NICE recommends early face-to-face review after starting, then regular review while titrating to an adequate dose.

Review at 2 weeks for most patients; at 1 week and then weekly if under 30 or at increased suicide risk.
Allow 4–6 weeks at an adequate dose before deciding a drug has failed.
On remission, continue at the same dose for at least 6 months (longer if recurrent).
Assess mood, side effects, adherence, alcohol/drug use and suicidal ideation at each visit.
3Interpretation & actions
No response after 4–6 weeks at therapeutic dose→Optimise (increase) dose, or switch antidepressant
Early worsening / agitation / suicidal ideation in young adults→Increase monitoring frequency, review urgently
Abrupt stop of SSRI/SNRI→Discontinuation syndrome (dizziness, flu-like, electric-shock sensations) — taper
SSRI + other serotonergic drug + agitation/clonus/hyperthermia→Serotonin syndrome
SSRI + NSAID or anticoagulant→GI bleed risk — consider gastroprotection (PPI)
Citalopram / escitalopram at high dose→QTc prolongation — ECG, dose limits
SSRI, especially in the elderly→Hyponatraemia (SIADH) — check sodium if symptomatic
4Pitfalls, safety & drug-specific harms
🧪Hyponatraemia
SIADH — confusion, falls; check Na⁺ in the elderly
🩸GI bleeding
Risk rises with NSAIDs/anticoagulants — add PPI
💓QTc prolongation
Citalopram/escitalopram; avoid other QT-prolonging drugs
🔁Discontinuation
Worse with short half-life (paroxetine, venlafaxine); taper
🚩 Serotonin syndrome — agitation, clonus, hyperreflexia, hyperthermia and autonomic instability — is a medical emergency: stop all serotonergic drugs, give supportive care (cooling, fluids, benzodiazepines) ± cyproheptadine. Watch for increased suicidality in the under-25s during the first weeks, and always taper to avoid discontinuation syndrome.
🎓 Allow 4–6 weeks at a therapeutic dose before judging failure; continue for 6 months after remission; taper when stopping. Remember SSRIs cause hyponatraemia and GI bleeding, and citalopram/escitalopram prolong the QTc.
THERAPEUTIC DRUG MONITORING__Drug Levels:
Digoxin is a cardiac glycoside used for ventricular rate control in atrial fibrillation and as an adjunct in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. It has a narrow therapeutic index, so serum level monitoring — interpreted alongside potassium, magnesium and renal function — is essential to steer between underdosing and life-threatening toxicity.

1Indication & principle

Digoxin inhibits the myocardial Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, raising intracellular calcium (positive inotropy) and enhancing vagal tone to slow AV nodal conduction (rate control). It is a second-line rate-control agent in AF, favoured in sedentary or hypotensive patients and in coexisting heart failure.

Renally excreted — accumulates in renal impairment and the elderly.
Narrow therapeutic index: therapeutic and toxic levels overlap, so a number alone never confirms toxicity.
Electrolytes (K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺) critically modulate its effect at the ATPase.
2How the level is sampled

Take the serum digoxin sample at least 6 hours post-dose (ideally 8–12 h) to allow distribution into tissues; earlier sampling gives a falsely high, uninterpretable result. Send paired U&Es, potassium and magnesium at the same time.

Sample <6 h post-dose→Falsely elevated (still in distribution phase) — do not act on it
Rising creatinine / falling eGFR→Reduced clearance — anticipate accumulation and toxicity
3Interpretation & cut-offs
0.8–2.0 micrograms/L (AF)→Usual therapeutic range
0.5–0.9 micrograms/L→Target in heart failure (lower levels improve outcomes)
>2.0 micrograms/L with symptoms→Digoxin toxicity likely — act clinically
Hypokalaemia at a ‘normal’ level→Toxicity can occur despite an in-range number

Toxicity is a clinical diagnosis. Recognise the features:

🤢GI upset
Nausea, vomiting, anorexia — often the earliest sign
👁️Xanthopsia
Yellow-green visual haloes; blurred vision, confusion
🐢Bradyarrhythmia
Bradycardia, AV block, SVT with AV block
⚡Bidirectional VT
Classic (near-pathognomonic) toxic arrhythmia
4Precipitants & pitfalls
Hypokalaemia (loop/thiazide diuretics)→Potentiates toxicity — low K⁺ frees the ATPase binding site
Hypomagnesaemia & hypercalcaemia→Increase myocardial sensitivity to digoxin
Amiodarone, verapamil, quinidine→Raise serum digoxin — reduce dose and re-check level
🚩 Digoxin toxicity is life-threatening. For significant arrhythmia, haemodynamic instability or hyperkalaemia, give DigiFab (digoxin-specific antibody fragments). Correct hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia, but never give calcium to treat the hyperkalaemia of digoxin toxicity. Watch diuretic co-prescription closely — hypokalaemia dramatically amplifies toxicity even when the digoxin number looks normal.
🎓 Sample ≥6 h post-dose; therapeutic range 0.8–2.0 micrograms/L (lower 0.5–0.9 in heart failure). Hypokalaemia potentiates toxicity. Yellow-green vision plus a new arrhythmia = toxicity until proven otherwise; the antidote is the digoxin-specific antibody DigiFab.

Phenytoin is a first-line anti-epileptic used for focal and generalised tonic-clonic seizures and as second-line control in status epilepticus. It has a narrow therapeutic index and, uniquely among common drugs, follows zero-order (saturable) kinetics at therapeutic doses — so therapeutic drug monitoring is essential to keep the patient in the safe window and to explain sudden toxicity after seemingly small dose changes.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE
Monitor because phenytoin has a narrow therapeutic index — the gap between an effective and a toxic level is small.
Metabolism is by hepatic enzymes that become saturated within the therapeutic range. Once saturated, elimination switches from first-order to zero-order: a fixed amount is cleared per hour regardless of concentration.
Consequence: a small dose increase can produce a disproportionately large rise in serum level, tipping a stable patient into toxicity.
Zero-order (saturable) kinetics→once enzymes saturated, a small dose increase → a large, non-linear level rise
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — SAMPLING
Take a trough level (pre-dose, immediately before the next dose) at steady state — usually after 5-7 days of a stable dose given the long half-life.
Routine levels are not needed once the patient is stable and seizure-free; check when toxicity is suspected, seizures recur, adherence is doubted, dose is changed, or in pregnancy.
Phenytoin is ~90% protein-bound to albumin, and laboratories report total drug. Always interpret alongside the serum albumin; correct the level or measure the free (unbound, active) fraction in hypoalbuminaemia, renal failure or pregnancy.
3INTERPRETATION — VALUES & TOXICITY
Therapeutic range 10-20 mg/L (40-80 µmol/L)→target for total phenytoin at normal albumin
Level >20 mg/L→nystagmus first, then ataxia, then drowsiness / confusion as levels climb further
Low albumin→total level underestimates the free (active) drug — a “normal” total may be toxic; use corrected or free level
Chronic exposure→gum hypertrophy, hirsutism, coarsened facies, folate deficiency, cerebellar atrophy, osteomalacia
Potent hepatic enzyme inducer→reduces efficacy of warfarin, the combined pill, DOACs and many other drugs
👁️Nystagmus
earliest sign of toxicity as level exceeds 20 mg/L
🚶Ataxia
cerebellar signs and unsteady gait with further rise
😴Drowsiness
confusion and reduced consciousness at high levels
🧪Albumin
needed to interpret the total level correctly
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Interpreting the total level without albumin is the classic trap — in hypoalbuminaemia the free drug is higher than the total suggests, so a “therapeutic” number can mask toxicity.
Because of zero-order kinetics, dose adjustments must be small (e.g. 25-50 mg steps) with re-check after steady state, not scaled linearly.
Numerous drug interactions (enzyme induction and displacement from albumin, e.g. valproate) alter levels and effect — review the whole drug chart.
🚩 IV phenytoin must be given slowly with continuous cardiac (ECG) and blood pressure monitoring — rapid infusion causes hypotension, bradycardia and arrhythmia. Because of zero-order kinetics, small dose changes can tip a patient into toxicity, so titrate cautiously and always correct levels for a low albumin before acting on them.
🎓 Range 10-20 mg/L; zero-order / saturable kinetics mean small dose rises cause large level jumps; toxicity sequence is nystagmus → ataxia → drowsiness; always correct for albumin (or measure free level); it is a strong enzyme inducer.

Theophylline (given intravenously as aminophylline, its ethylenediamine salt) is a methylxanthine bronchodilator with a narrow therapeutic index, used in severe asthma and COPD when first-line therapy fails. Because the gap between the effective and the toxic dose is small, serum levels must be measured to keep the patient in range and to avoid life-threatening toxicity.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Used as an add-on bronchodilator in acute severe/life-threatening asthma or exacerbations of COPD not responding to nebulised beta-agonists, ipratropium and steroids. It inhibits phosphodiesterase (raising cyclic AMP) and antagonises adenosine, producing bronchodilation and central respiratory stimulation.

The narrow window between benefit and harm is the whole reason monitoring is mandatory.
Clearance varies hugely between patients (smoking, age, drugs, liver disease), so a fixed dose gives unpredictable levels.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — SAMPLING

For an IV aminophylline infusion, take the level 4–6 hours after starting the infusion (once quasi-steady state is reached); if the infusion is continuing, a further level can guide rate adjustment. For oral modified-release theophylline, take a trough level just before the next dose (typically ~5 days after starting or dose change).

🚩 Always take a level BEFORE giving an IV aminophylline loading dose to a patient already taking oral theophylline — loading on top of an existing level can push into the toxic range and precipitate a fatal event.
3INTERPRETATION & CUT-OFFS
10–20 mg/L (55–110 µmol/L)→Therapeutic range — target for efficacy with acceptable safety
<10 mg/L→Sub-therapeutic — inadequate bronchodilation; consider inducers/non-adherence
>20 mg/L→Toxicity — nausea/vomiting, tachycardia/arrhythmia, agitation, seizures
Toxicity with hypokalaemia→Beta-agonist-like K⁺ shift into cells — monitor and replace potassium
🧪Ciprofloxacin
Enzyme inhibitor — RAISES level
🧪Macrolides
Erythromycin/clarithromycin RAISE level
🧪Cimetidine
Enzyme inhibitor — RAISES level
🚬Smoking
Enzyme inducer — LOWERS level
💊Rifampicin
Enzyme inducer — LOWERS level
💊Phenytoin
Enzyme inducer — LOWERS level
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
The narrow window means small dose or clearance changes cause large swings — a “normal” regimen can become toxic when a macrolide or quinolone is added.
Toxicity is not just gastrointestinal — hypokalaemia, tachyarrhythmias and seizures can occur with little warning and may be the first sign.
Levels must be interpreted with timing: an early post-infusion sample or a non-trough oral level misleads.
🎓 Therapeutic range 10–20 mg/L. Toxicity triad to remember: hypokalaemia + tachyarrhythmia + seizures. Smoking LOWERS levels; ciprofloxacin and macrolides RAISE them. Always check a level before IV loading if the patient is already on oral theophylline.

Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) of gentamicin (an aminoglycoside) and vancomycin (a glycopeptide) uses timed serum drug concentrations to guide dosing of narrow-therapeutic-index antibiotics. Both drugs are potently effective against serious infections but nephrotoxic, and gentamicin is additionally ototoxic, so levels are measured to keep the patient in the therapeutic window: high enough to kill the organism, low enough to avoid toxicity.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Gentamicin is used for serious Gram-negative sepsis, and vancomycin for MRSA and other Gram-positive infections including C. difficile (oral) and endocarditis. Both have a narrow therapeutic index with wide inter-patient variability driven largely by renal clearance, so a standard mg/kg dose does not reliably predict serum concentration.

Aminoglycoside killing is concentration-dependent with a post-antibiotic effect — a high peak drives efficacy, while a low trough allows drug washout and limits toxic tissue accumulation.
Vancomycin killing is time-dependent (exposure-driven), so efficacy relates to the AUC/MIC ratio, approximated in practice by the pre-dose trough level.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Gentamicin is usually given as once-daily (extended-interval) dosing based on ideal body weight. A single level is drawn at a set time after the dose (commonly 6–14 h) and plotted on a nomogram (e.g. Hartford) to decide the dosing interval; alternatively a formal peak-and-trough regimen is used in endocarditis, pregnancy or significant renal impairment.

Vancomycin is dosed by weight and renal function; a pre-dose trough is checked (typically before the 3rd or 4th dose, once near steady state), or dosing is AUC-guided where available.
Always record the exact time the dose was given and the exact time the sample was taken — a mistimed level is uninterpretable and is the commonest source of error.
3INTERPRETATION

The trough tells you about accumulation and toxicity risk; the peak (where measured) tells you about efficacy.

Gentamicin pre-dose trough <1 mg/L (extended interval) / <2 mg/L (multiple daily)→Acceptable — give next dose
Gentamicin trough above target→Accumulation — hold dose / extend interval, do not simply re-dose
Gentamicin high trough + rising creatinine→Nephrotoxicity — reduce or hold, review other nephrotoxins
Vancomycin trough 10–20 mg/L (15–20 for serious MRSA)→Therapeutic target range
Vancomycin trough <10 mg/L→Subtherapeutic — risk of treatment failure and resistance, increase dose
Vancomycin trough >20 mg/L→Supratherapeutic — nephrotoxicity risk, reduce dose
🧪Trough (pre-dose)
Lowest level, just before next dose — reflects accumulation and toxicity risk
📈Peak
Post-dose maximum — reflects efficacy for concentration-dependent gentamicin
📊Nomogram / AUC
Hartford nomogram sets gentamicin interval; AUC/MIC guides vancomycin exposure
4PITFALLS & SAFETY
A sample drawn too early (before the true trough) reads falsely high and may lead to inappropriately withholding an effective dose; a sample drawn too late reads falsely low and may mask accumulation.
Gentamicin causes irreversible ototoxicity and vestibulotoxicity (deafness, oscillopsia, imbalance) — this is cumulative and can occur even with normal levels, so total exposure and duration matter.
Vancomycin infused too rapidly causes red man syndrome, a histamine-mediated flush of the face, neck and trunk — it is a rate-related reaction, not a true allergy, and is prevented by slowing the infusion (over at least 60 min).
🚩 Aminoglycosides are nephrotoxic and cause IRREVERSIBLE ototoxicity and vestibular damage. Monitor trough levels and renal function, avoid in renal impairment where possible and alongside other nephrotoxins. A raised trough means the next dose should be withheld or delayed — NOT given.
🎓 Gentamicin: extended-interval dosing, keep trough <1 mg/L, remember it is nephrotoxic and ototoxic. Vancomycin: target trough 15–20 mg/L for serious MRSA and infuse slowly to avoid red man syndrome.

Ciclosporin and tacrolimus are calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs) — potent immunosuppressants with a narrow therapeutic index. Because the gap between too little drug (graft rejection) and too much (organ toxicity) is small and inter-patient handling varies widely, they demand therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) on whole-blood pre-dose trough levels to steer dosing after solid-organ transplant and in refractory autoimmune disease.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

CNIs block calcineurin, preventing IL-2 transcription and T-cell activation. They are core agents for prevention of transplant rejection (kidney, liver, heart, lung) and for severe autoimmune disease (e.g. steroid-refractory ulcerative colitis, atopic dermatitis, nephrotic syndrome). Monitoring is mandatory because the therapeutic window is narrow, absorption is erratic, and both under- and over-exposure carry serious consequences.

Too little drug → the immune system is under-suppressed → graft rejection.
Too much drug → dose-dependent nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity and hypertension.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — SAMPLING

The standard measurement is the whole-blood trough level (C0), taken immediately before the next dose (both drugs partition heavily into red cells, so whole blood, not plasma, is used). Timing is critical — a sample drawn too early overestimates exposure.

Sample type→EDTA whole blood, pre-dose (trough / C0)
Timing→Just before dose, ~12 h after the previous dose

Target tacrolimus troughs fall over time post-transplant — higher early (e.g. ~10–15 ng/mL in the first weeks) and lower for long-term maintenance (~5–8 ng/mL) as rejection risk declines.

3INTERPRETATION
Subtherapeutic trough→Under-immunosuppression → risk of graft rejection
Supratherapeutic trough→Nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity (tremor), hypertension
Tacrolimus specifically→New-onset diabetes, tremor, hyperkalaemia
Ciclosporin specifically→Gum (gingival) hypertrophy, hirsutism

Distinctive class members and their trademark toxicities:

🧪Tacrolimus
Nephrotoxic; new-onset diabetes, tremor, hyperkalaemia
🧪Ciclosporin
Nephrotoxic; gum hypertrophy, hirsutism
⬆️CYP3A4 inhibitors
Macrolides, azoles, diltiazem, grapefruit → raise levels → toxicity
⬇️CYP3A4 inducers
Rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, St John's Wort → lower levels → rejection
4PITFALLS & SAFETY

Both CNIs are heavily metabolised by hepatic CYP3A4, so drug and food interactions dominate their pharmacokinetics and are a frequent cause of levels drifting out of range.

CYP3A4 inhibitor added (e.g. clarithromycin, itraconazole, diltiazem, grapefruit)→Levels rise → nephro-/neurotoxicity
CYP3A4 inducer added (e.g. rifampicin, St John's Wort)→Levels fall → rejection risk
🚩 CNIs are themselves nephrotoxic, so a rising creatinine in a transplant patient may be rejection OR drug toxicity — the two are told apart by the measured level (low favours rejection, high favours toxicity), often with biopsy. Beware CYP3A4 interactions: azoles, macrolides and grapefruit juice can push levels into the toxic range, while rifampicin and St John's Wort can drop them into the rejection range.
🎓 Monitor on the whole-blood pre-dose trough. Both CNIs are nephrotoxic; remember the fingerprints — tacrolimus = diabetes + tremor, ciclosporin = gum hypertrophy + hirsutism. CYP3A4 interactions dominate: inhibitors up, inducers down.

Anticoagulation monitoring and reversal is the coagulation-lab and bedside toolkit used to check that a patient is anticoagulated in a safe therapeutic window and to rapidly undo that anticoagulation when they bleed or need urgent surgery. Warfarin is monitored with the INR, low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) and direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are not routinely monitored but can be assessed with anti-Xa assays, and emergency reversal relies on vitamin K, prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) and specific DOAC antidotes.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Anticoagulants inhibit clotting to prevent or treat thrombosis (AF stroke prevention, VTE, mechanical valves), but the therapeutic margin is narrow: too little and the patient clots, too much and they bleed. Warfarin blocks vitamin-K-dependent factors (II, VII, IX, X), so its effect is variable and dose is titrated to the INR — a standardised ratio of the prothrombin time. LMWH and DOACs have predictable pharmacokinetics and need no routine monitoring, but their effect can be quantified with an anti-Xa assay when the level is genuinely in doubt.

Warfarin → monitored with INR.
LMWH / DOACs → predictable, no routine monitoring.
Reversal needed for major bleeding or urgent surgery.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

The INR is derived from a venous prothrombin time and reported as a unitless ratio; warfarin patients are checked frequently during induction and then at intervals up to 12 weeks once stable. LMWH usually needs no test, but a peak anti-Xa level (taken 4 hours post-dose) is used in renal impairment, extremes of body weight and pregnancy. DOACs need no routine test; a drug-specific calibrated anti-Xa assay (for apixaban/rivaroxaban) or a dilute thrombin time (for dabigatran) is reserved for bleeding, urgent surgery or suspected accumulation.

🧪INR
Standardised PT ratio for warfarin.
🩸Anti-Xa
Quantifies LMWH and Xa-inhibitor DOACs.
⏱️Peak timing
LMWH anti-Xa taken 4 h post-dose.
💊dTT
Dilute thrombin time gauges dabigatran.
3INTERPRETATION & TARGETS

Warfarin targets depend on indication: INR 2.0–3.0 for AF and VTE, and a higher 2.5–3.5 for mechanical heart valves or recurrent VTE on treatment. A raised INR is managed by how high it is and whether the patient is bleeding.

INR 2.0–3.0→Therapeutic for AF / VTE
INR 2.5–3.5→Target for mechanical valve / recurrent VTE
INR raised but <8, no bleeding→Withhold 1–2 warfarin doses, reduce maintenance, recheck
INR ≥8, no or minor bleeding→Stop warfarin + oral vitamin K, recheck INR
Major bleeding on warfarin→STOP warfarin, IV vitamin K + PCC (Beriplex) — not FFP first-line
Dabigatran major bleed→Idarucizumab
Apixaban / rivaroxaban major bleed→Andexanet alfa or PCC
4PITFALLS & SAFETY

The INR only reflects warfarin (and liver synthetic function) — it does not reliably measure DOACs, so a normal INR never excludes a therapeutic or supratherapeutic DOAC level. Anti-Xa assays must be calibrated to the specific drug being measured, and heparin-calibrated assays cannot be read as a DOAC concentration. Vitamin K given IV works over 6–12 hours, which is too slow for life-threatening bleeding, hence the need for immediate clotting-factor replacement with PCC.

A normal INR does not exclude DOAC effect.
Anti-Xa must be drug-specifically calibrated.
IV vitamin K is too slow to rely on alone in major bleeding.
🚩 Major bleeding on warfarin is reversed with IV vitamin K PLUS prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC, e.g. Beriplex) — PCC restores factors II, VII, IX, X faster and more completely than FFP, so do NOT simply give FFP first-line. For DOACs, know the specific antidotes: idarucizumab for dabigatran, and andexanet alfa (or PCC) for the factor Xa inhibitors apixaban and rivaroxaban.
🎓 Warfarin INR target is 2.0–3.0 (2.5–3.5 for mechanical valves). Major bleed = STOP warfarin + IV vitamin K + PCC (not FFP). Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran; andexanet alfa reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban.
